sections.text:
Let us now examine our common conceptions concerning the Spirit: those gathered from the Scriptures and those handed down to us from the unwritten tradition of the fathers.

First, who hears the titles of the Spirit and is not lifted up in soul, raising thought toward the highest nature? He is called “Spirit of God,” “Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father,” “right Spirit,” and “ruling Spirit.” His principal and distinctive name is “Holy Spirit,” a name especially fitting to what is incorporeal, purely simple, and indivisible.

Therefore the Lord, teaching the woman who thought God must be worshiped in a particular place that the incorporeal cannot be circumscribed, said, “God is Spirit.” When we hear “Spirit,” then, it is impossible to conceive a nature bounded by limits, subject to change and alteration, or in any way like created nature. We are compelled to advance in thought toward what is highest: an intelligent essence, infinite in power, unlimited in greatness, not measured by times or ages, unstinting in the good things it possesses.

Toward him turn all things needing sanctification; after him reach all who live according to virtue, as though watered by his breath and assisted toward their own proper and natural end. He perfects others and is himself deficient in nothing. He lives not by being repaired or replenished but is the Giver of life. He does not increase by additions but is full at once, established in himself and present everywhere.

He is the source of sanctification, intelligible light, providing through himself a kind of illumination to every rational power seeking truth. By nature inaccessible, yet approachable through goodness; filling all things by power, yet participated in only by the worthy; not shared in one measure but distributing his activity according to the proportion of faith.

Simple in essence, manifold in powers, wholly present to each and wholly everywhere; divided without suffering division and participated in without ceasing to remain whole. It is like a sunbeam: to the one who enjoys it, it seems present for that one alone, yet it illuminates land and sea and mingles with the air. So too the Spirit is present to each receptive person as though to that person alone, yet supplies grace sufficient and undiminished to all. Those who participate enjoy him according to the capacity of their own nature, not according to the measure of his power.

The Spirit's intimacy with the soul is not a local approach—for how could one draw bodily near to what is incorporeal? It comes through separation from the passions, which afterward attached themselves to the soul through its friendship with the flesh and alienated it from closeness to God.

Only after a person has been purified from the shame with which wickedness stained the soul and has returned to the beauty belonging to its nature—like restoring to a royal image its ancient form through cleansing—can one draw near to the Paraclete.

Then he, like the sun taking hold of a purified eye, will show you in himself the image of the Invisible; and in the blessed contemplation of the Image you will behold the ineffable beauty of the Archetype.

Through the Spirit comes the ascent of hearts, the guiding of the weak by the hand, and the perfecting of those who advance. Shining upon those cleansed from every stain, he makes them spiritual through communion with himself.

Just as bright and transparent bodies become radiant when a sunbeam falls upon them and themselves emit another brightness, so souls bearing the Spirit, illumined by the Spirit, become spiritual and send grace outward to others.

From this come foreknowledge of things to come, understanding of mysteries, comprehension of hidden things, distribution of gifts, heavenly citizenship, the chorus with angels, joy without end, abiding in God, likeness to God, and—highest of all the things desired—becoming godlike by grace.

These, to mention a few among many, are the conceptions concerning the Holy Spirit that we have been taught from the Spirit's own oracles concerning his greatness, dignity, and operations.

translator_notes: Direct Mercy translation from Basil's Greek PG 32 text.
The final phrase of §23 expresses patristic deification/theosis: participation by grace, not identity with the divine essence.
Basil combines scriptural testimony with unwritten patristic tradition while describing the Spirit's divinity and sanctifying work.
